slides.title: Where the margin went
Gross margin and e-commerce fulfillment explain 79% of the margin decline; store labor explains only 13%

claims.claim: 78.8% of the 2.35 percentage-point decline came from gross margin and e-commerce fulfillment
evidence: Chart: FY2023 margin 3.37%; Gross margin −1.019 pp; Store labor −0.30 pp; Occupancy and energy −0.199 pp; E-commerce fulfillment −0.838 pp; FY2025 margin 1.02%
Other SG&A stayed at 4.7% of sales and is not shown

claims.claim: Gross margin: deeper promotions and higher shrink, not supplier costs, took it down
E-commerce fulfillment: cost more than tripled to $18.1M as orders grew 2.9 times and more went to the home
Store labor: the cause management names is only the third-largest of the four
evidence: Store labor's share of the decline 12.7%

slides.title: Promotions and shrink cost $18M of FY2025 gross profit, far more than private label added

claims.claim: $18.04M of FY2025 gross profit lost to the rise in promotions and shrink, at FY2025 sales
evidence: Chart: FY2023 gross margin 26.04%; Promotional mix −0.70 pp; Private-label mix +0.18 pp; Shrink −0.50 pp; FY2025 gross margin 25.02%
the three drivers account for the whole 1.02 percentage-point fall

claims.claim: Promotional mix: 29% of sales now sell on promotion, up from 24%, each dollar at 14 percentage points less margin
evidence: vendor funding fell from 55% to 46% of markdowns

claims.claim: Private label: share rose from 17% to 18.5% of sales at 12 percentage points more margin, too little to offset
Shrink: fresh and produce waste is 45% of it and receiving or admin errors 20%, both tied to store work

slides.title: Productivity has absorbed most wage inflation: hourly cost rose 9.4%, but hours per sales dollar fell 6%

claims.claim: The cost pressure management describes is real
evidence: Average hourly wage including benefits +9.4%
$16.80 an hour in FY2023, $18.38 in FY2025
State minimum wage and a tight labor market, as the CFO and COO say
Another 4% minimum-wage rise is due in 2027

claims.claim: Stores already absorbed most of the wage rise
evidence: Labor hours per thousand dollars of sales −5.98%
7.02 hours in FY2023, 6.60 in FY2025
Labor cost per sales dollar rose only 2.5%
Managers of the leanest stores say rotation and receiving checks are skipped on busy days

claims.claim: The smallest of the three large causes of the decline
evidence: Store labor as a share of sales +0.3 pp
11.8% of sales in FY2023, 12.1% in FY2025
13% of the operating-margin decline
The proposed 8% hours cut, worth about $14.5M a year, targets this line

slides.title: Promotions and shrink
Deeper promotions have not protected Harlow's price image: promo share rose to 29% while 'more expensive' rose to 41%

claims.claim: Promotions grew every year, from 24% to 29% of sales
evidence: +5 pp
Promotional share: FY2023 24%; FY2024 26.2%; FY2025 29%

claims.claim: Yet more shoppers now see Harlow as the expensive option
evidence: +8 pp
More expensive: FY2023 33%; FY2025 41%
Customer survey, n = 3,100 (FY2025)

claims.claim: Category managers deepened promotions to defend traffic against ValuMart, yet 38% of FY2025 events lost money even after their extra units

slides.title: Price investment belongs in ValuMart's trade areas, not in network-wide promotions that do not pay back

claims.claim: ValuMart's pressure is local: Harlow stores near its 11 new stores fell 4.2%
evidence: Comparable sales growth FY2025: Within 3 miles of a new ValuMart −4.2%; Other Harlow stores +1.1%

claims.claim: Deep-promotion stores grew faster, but the gain pays for only 2.3 percentage points more promo share
evidence: Deepest promotions +1.8%; Other stores +0.2%
Break-even: 1.6 percentage points of extra sales × 20 cents per new dollar ÷ 14 percentage points of margin gap = 2.3 percentage points of promo share

claims.claim: Fund local price moves near ValuMart from the promotion savings

slides.title: Cutting money-losing events to bring promotions back to their FY2023 share of sales would add about $9.9M a year

claims.claim: Promotional reset adds $9.9M more operating income a year
evidence: 5 pp of sales moves back from promotional to regular price: 29% today, 24% in FY2023
× 14 pp less gross margin on each promoted dollar
× $1,414.5M continuing-store sales, FY2025 base, after the nine store exits

claims.claim: The reset is cautious: it removes fewer than half of the money-losing events
evidence: 38% of FY2025 events lost money after counting their extra units; if events are similar in size they carry about 11 percentage points of sales, more than twice the 5 to remove

claims.claim: Dropping an event that loses money raises profit by definition; the risk is traffic, which belongs in ValuMart trade areas
The 14 percentage-point margin gap holds; winning vendor funding back from 46% toward 55% of markdowns is upside, not counted
Each percentage point of promotional share left in place costs about $1.98M a year

slides.title: Cutting hours would feed shrink: the leanest-staffed stores lose 3.1% of sales to it, against 2.3% in the best-staffed

claims.claim: Shrink falls as hours rise, up to the best-staffed quartile
evidence: Shrink % of sales: Q1 fewest hours 3.1%; Q2 2.7%; Q3 2.4%; Q4 most hours 2.3%
Network, FY2025 2.6%
Q1: fewest hours: rotation and receiving checks get skipped on busy days
Labor-driven: waste and receiving errors are 65% of shrink
Q4: only 0.1 percentage points below Q3, so extra hours buy little

claims.claim: Expected gain if every quartile reached Q4's 2.3%: $4.6M
evidence: (2.63% quartile average − 2.3%) × $1,414.5M continuing sales

slides.title: E-commerce and weak stores
Counted in full, e-commerce loses $10.4M a year; the team's reported profit leaves out delivery and cannibalization

claims.claim: Delivery drives the loss, and most online spend is not new
evidence: Chart ($M, FY2025): Picking cost 9.85; Delivery net of fees 8.26; Contribution from new sales −7.67; Net cost to Harlow 10.44

claims.claim: Delivery net of fees: the carrier costs $13.80 per delivered order and the fee brings in $3.10; the team's 6.1% margin leaves it out
evidence: Picking = 1,331,000 orders × $7.40; delivery = 772,000 delivered orders × ($13.80 − $3.10)

claims.claim: Contribution from new sales: 70% of online spend would have been spent in a Harlow store anyway
evidence: survey of 2,300 customers
Contribution = $127.8M e-commerce sales × 30% new to Harlow × 20 cents per new dollar (finance)

claims.claim: Per order: a delivered order loses about $12.34 and a click-and-collect order $1.64, so growth in delivery deepens the loss

slides.title: Rolling out the tested delivery fee would cut the e-commerce loss by about $2.5M a year and keep the service

claims.claim: $2.5M smaller e-commerce loss a year, with delivery still offered
evidence: $3M lower picking and delivery cost net of fees: delivered orders −9%, click-and-collect +14%, $6.40 fee per delivered order (fee test)
− $0.5M contribution lost on 2% lower e-commerce sales, all treated as new to Harlow

claims.claim: The test is small, so the rollout should be tracked against it
evidence: The 4-store, 10-week result holds network-wide: a $7.99 fee and free delivery from $100, instead of $4.99 and $75
Picking stays at $7.40 an order and the carrier at $13.80; its proposed 3% rise is counted separately in the plan
Treating every lost sale as new overstates the cost: at the survey's 30% new share it would be about $0.15M

claims.claim: After the rollout e-commerce still costs about $7.96M a year: carrier terms and a shift to click-and-collect come next
The owners want delivery kept in some form; repricing keeps it while 98% of e-commerce sales stay in the test

slides.title: Exiting the nine loss-making stores would add about $6.6M a year; six leases end by 2027 without a board vote

claims.claim: $6.6M more operating income a year once all nine are closed
evidence: $3.1M four-wall EBITDA losses of the nine stores removed (FY2025)
+ $3.5M contribution on the 25% of their $118.0M sales that moves to nearby Harlow stores, at 12%

claims.claim: Three of the nine need a board vote and use $7.5M of the $25M capital limit
evidence: Six leases end by the end of 2027 and can be exited as they lapse
The other three need a board vote and a one-time $7.5M lease exit, leaving $17.5M of the limit
Split evenly, those three add about $2.21M a year and pay back the exit cost in about 3.4 years

claims.claim: The exits remove $88.5M of sales, which lowers the sales base for the 3.0% target

slides.title: Plan and first moves
The five actions reach the 3.0% target by FY2028 before the 2027 wage rise, and about 2.5% after it

claims.claim: How the five actions add up
evidence: Chart ($M): FY2025 15.3; Promotions +9.9; Shrink +4.6; Delivery fee +2.49; Store exits +6.64; Private label +3.82; Wage and carrier rises −7.14; FY2028 35.61

claims.claim: 3.02% FY2028 margin before the cost rises
evidence: $42.75M ÷ $1,414.5M continuing sales

claims.claim: FY2028 margin after them 2.5%
evidence: Range: 2.2% if promotions fall only to 26.2%; 2.7% if shrink returns to 2.1%

claims.claim: The wage rise is the gap to the target
evidence: Cut in store hours that would offset both rises 4.2%
$7.1M ÷ $1.7M per 1% of hours
Wage rise = 4% × $171.2M store labor; carrier = 3% × $13.80 × 702,500 orders; private label +0.75 percentage points a year × 3 years × 12 percentage points

slides.title: Management's hours cut protects the covenant, but shrink and the wage rise would erase its saving by FY2028

claims.claim: Net gain left by FY2028: effectively nothing
evidence: $14.5M saving a year from 8% fewer scheduled store hours (management estimate)
− $7.5M gross profit lost if shrink rises 0.5 pp of sales, as it did when hours per sales dollar fell 6%
− $6.7M 2027 minimum-wage rise of 4% on the remaining store labor
− $0.3M carrier's proposed 3% rise, with e-commerce frozen at today's size

claims.claim: The cut is fast, which is why it appeals, but it leaves the real causes in place
evidence: In FY2026 the plan would bring operating income to $22–29.5M, clear of the $20M covenant
By FY2028 margin would sit at 1.0–1.5% of sales; the high end assumes shrink does not rise at all
The freeze keeps the e-commerce loss of about $10.4M a year, and promotions and shrink are untouched

claims.claim: A smaller cut of about 4% of hours, taken only from the most-staffed stores after shrink is fixed, is the better use of the idea
evidence: the leanest quartile already runs 0.8 percentage points above the best-staffed

claims.claim: Keep a targeted hours cut as the lever that closes the gap to 3.0%, not as the plan's first move

slides.title: The first wave would lift FY2026 operating income to about $25M, above the $20M covenant

claims.claim: The first wave turns the trend and leaves about $5.2M of headroom
evidence: Covenant minimum, FY2026 $20.0M
$15.3M FY2025 operating income + $10.2M first-wave actions in FY2026 − $0.3M carrier's proposed 3% rise at the 2026 renewal = $25.2M FY2026 estimate
First wave = half the promotion reset ($5.26M) + half the shrink gain ($2.44M) + delivery fee ($2.49M)

claims.claim: FY2023–FY2025: operating income fell by $14.5M and then $18.1M a year, mainly through promotions, shrink and delivery
FY2026E: the covenant holds if the first wave delivers at least 49% of its value
Risk: a further slide in the base business of more than $5.2M before the actions land would breach it
Start the three no-capital moves at once and report the covenant forecast to the lender monthly

slides.title: Next steps

normalized.recommendation: Fix promotions, shrink and delivery pricing before cutting hours. Start the three no-capital moves at once and report the covenant forecast to the lender monthly; exit the nine loss-making stores (six as leases end, three after board vote); keep a targeted hours cut as the lever that closes the gap to 3.0%, not as the plan's first move. Ask the board now for the plan and the three store-exit votes; targeted hours wait for the FY2027 gate.

alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected as the first move: protects the covenant (FY2026 operating income $22–29.5M) but shrink and the wage rise would erase its saving by FY2028 (net −$0.02M); FY2028 margin would sit at 1.0–1.5%; it leaves the real causes in place. Next steps: Stop the 8% hours cut.

alternatives_considered.option: Targeted hours cut of about 4%, only from the most-staffed stores after shrink is fixed
alternatives_considered.treatment: Chosen as a later lever: 'the better use of the idea'; closes the gap to 3.0%, subject to the FY2027 gate.

alternatives_considered.option: Network-wide (chain-wide) promotions to defend against ValuMart
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected: network-wide promotions do not pay back; price investment belongs in ValuMart's trade areas, funded from the promotion savings.

alternatives_considered.option: Freezing e-commerce at today's size (part of management's draft plan)
alternatives_considered.treatment: Rejected implicitly: the freeze keeps the e-commerce loss of about $10.4M a year. Deck instead recommends rolling out the tested delivery fee, which keeps delivery (owners want delivery kept in some form).

assumptions_and_uncertainties: Synthetic benchmark data; all figures from the briefing pack
Run-rate at FY2025 cost ratios and continuing-store sales; interactions and sales growth ignored
FY2028 margin range: 2.2% if promotions fall only to 26.2%; 2.7% if shrink returns to 2.1%
Promotion reset: assumes the 14 percentage-point margin gap holds; vendor funding recovery is upside, not counted; if events are similar in size they carry about 11 pp of sales; the risk is traffic
The pack gives neither the deep-promotion stores' promo share nor how many stores sit near a ValuMart
Shrink gain: the pack does not give each quartile's sales, so the gain assumes equal sales; theft (35% of shrink) is not addressed
Delivery fee: the test is small (4-store, 10-week) and the result is assumed to hold network-wide; picking stays at $7.40 and carrier at $13.80; treating every lost sale as new overstates the cost

Store exits: per-store results are not in the briefing pack; closure costs for the six lapsing leases are not given and would also count against the $25M limit; exits remove $88.5M of sales, lowering the sales base for the 3.0% target
Management plan shrink risk uses the FY2023–25 pattern; high end of 1.0–1.5% assumes shrink does not rise at all
FY2026 covenant holds if the first wave delivers at least 49% of its value; a further slide in the base business of more than $5.2M before the actions land would breach it
2027 minimum-wage rise of 4% and carrier's proposed 3% rise
next_steps: Approve the plan, the three store-exit votes and the $7.5M lease-exit budget — CEO and board — February 2027 board meeting
Drop money-losing promotion events and reopen vendor-funding terms — Category team and CFO — FY2026 H1
Stop the 8% hours cut; restore produce rotation and receiving checks in the leanest stores — COO — FY2026 H1
Roll out the tested delivery fee and negotiate the carrier renewal — E-commerce team — FY2026 H1
Track the covenant monthly; bring a targeted hours plan to the FY2027 gate — CFO and COO — Monthly; FY2027 H1 gate
normalized.extraction_notes: Deck provided as plain text; no images to view. Waterfall chart values were taken from the 'base' and value series in the extraction; the signs of the step values (increase or decrease) come from the chart layout and titles, not from signed data. Slide 20's Gantt layout came through as flat text, so which half-year each activity falls in could not be recovered exactly. Some stated figures differ slightly in rounding (e.g. delivery fee $2.5M vs $2.49M, store exits $6.6M vs $6.64M); they are kept as given.
